title: Rav Mesharshiya bar Rav
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Yuchasin reports that he lived in the time of R' Huna son of Rav Yehoshua, from the chapter Osin Pasin; in Seder HaDorot it is written, ‘We have not found [this].’ But Hyman says Yuchasin is right, for in Eruvin 25a (supplied כה.) ‘Rav Abba (avuha), of Rav son of Rav Mesharshiya, said to them (the Rabbis).’ Hyman calls the Dikdukei Soferim reading very correct: ‘Rav, the father of Rav Mesharshiya son of Rav’; he says they erased the word avuha without justification. This phrasing is found several times in the Talmud, as in Pesachim 116b: ‘Rav Natan, the father of R' Huna son of Rav Natan,’ and likewise Chagigah 5b and Keritot 25b. Hyman says Yuchasin had this reading. Hyman says he reported in the name of Rava and quotes Amemar’s incomplete ‘hu de-havyin,’ etc., in this connection. Hyman therefore concludes that he was indeed in the time of R' Huna son of R' Yehoshua, who was also a student of Rava.

notes.text: Hyman compares two nested genealogical readings: Rav Abba (the father) of Rav son of Rav Mesharshiya, and Rav, father of Rav Mesharshiya son of Rav. The precise attachment remains difficult. Amemar’s hu de-havyin is quoted incompletely.

R-H is contextually Huna in the first Huna-son-of-explicit-Rav-Yehoshua phrase, the Natan example and the closing parallel; final R-Y is contextually Yehoshua. The abbreviated titles remain R-prime at those occurrences: the full title from another occurrence or the Keritot example is not transferred. Every explicit Rav remains, including both heading components. Hyman’s Yuchasin-is-right, very-correct, unjustified-erasure and indeed-in-that-time judgments retain their force as his argument, not admitted genealogy or manuscript history. The two whole saved Eruvin 24a scalars read Rav Abba, father of Rav son of Rav Mesharshiya; Wikisource encloses avuha in parentheses. They stand beside supplied 25a and old machine 24a without repairing Hebrew or proving why parentheses were used. Hyman’s preferred reading instead starts Rav, father of Rav Mesharshiya son of Rav. The precise attachment stays unresolved. Whole Chagigah 5b and Keritot 25b scalars support comparable father-of-son phrasing only; their full titles do not establish this family’s identities. The earlier bounded Eruvin 24b/25a/25b and Pesachim 116a–b nonmatches remain historical, not global absence; the Pesachim Natan example, uninspected Seder HaDorot search snippet and Amemar’s incomplete hu de-havyin are not newly verified. Osin Pasin is the contextual Eruvin chapter, not the earlier Pesachim suggestion. Yuchasin, Seder HaDorot and Dikdukei Soferim are contextual work labels; no edition collation or identity merge is admitted. We have not found is the quoted work’s plural observation, and all etc. truncations remain. The source hold and every older note remain unchanged.

The consulted scan of Hyman, volume III, printed p. 913, gives Eruvin כד. (24a), whereas the supplied transcription retained here gives כה. (25a). It retains his strongly preferred alternative father-chain and his criticism of the erased word. Davidson and Wikisource Eruvin 24a instead read Rav Abba, father of Rav son of Rav Mesharshiya; the alternative quoted from Dikdukei Soferim remains Hyman’s report, without merging the people in the two chains. The named Eruvin quotation ends the current 24a folio. Its continuation at 24b has Amemar’s והוא דחזיין לתשמישתא, a condition that the water be fit for use, followed by Rav Ashi’s qualification and the Gemara’s rejection. Thus the directly consulted continuation concerns the water ruling, not an independent statement about Mesharshiya’s lifetime or family. The printed notice’s והוא דחזיין agrees with the directly consulted continuation, whereas the supplied transcription has הוא דהויין; that supplied wording is retained in the translation. His Pesachim example, Yuchasin dating and exact Dikdukei Soferim and Seder HaDorot printings have not been independently collated here. The earlier notes describe the state before this printed-page and continuation inspection; Hyman’s chronological conclusion remains his argument.
